"Every sudoku wi ane answer can be solved by reasonin; guessin is never needed and rarely helps. Thir are the weys o reasonin this app can recognise and explain, easiest first. Whaur ane o them applies tae the puzzle ye hae open, it\'ll show ye every place it does."

"Find a cell wi juist twa or three candidates left - the fewer the better, and the busier the row, column and box roond it the better still.

Pick ane o its candidates and pencil it in lichtly. Noo follae the consequences: that digit is gane fae awthing the cell can see, which may leave ane o thae cells wi a single candidate, which forces anither, and sae on. Keep gaun.

Ane o twa things happens. Either it peters oot, and ye've learnt naething - rub it oot and try the ither candidate. Or ye reach a cell wi nae candidates left at aw, or a row wi naewhaur tae pit some digit. That's impossible, sae the digit ye pencilled in wis wrang, and ye can rule it oot for guid.

This is the ane tae reach for when awthing else has dried up. It's slower and it's record-keepin raither than pattern-spottin, but it can uncover moves the patterns miss. Ane elimination is aften eneuch tae start the easy techniques workin again; some positions still need a deeper search."

"Find twa cells wi the same twa candidates, say {3,7}, that cannae see ane anither - they're usually naewhaur near ane anither.

Noo look for a row, column or box whaur 7 has juist twa possible cells, ane o which is seen by the first o yer pair and the ither by the second. That's the link.

Ane o thae twa cells is the 7. Whichever it is, the cell o yer pair that sees it cannae be 7, sae it maun be 3. Ye dinnae ken which end is the 3, juist that ane o them is - and that's eneuch tae rule 3 oot o every cell that sees baith ends.

The hard pairt is the link, sae hunt for it the ither wey roond: mark the units whaur a digit has juist twa places first, then look for a matchin pair on either side."

"Hunt for cells wi exactly twa candidates - a Y-wing is made o three o them and naething else.

Tak ane as the pivot, say {2,5}. Look for a cell it can see haudin {2,9}, and anither it can see haudin {5,9}. The pivot is either 2 or 5. If it's 2, the first pincer maun be 9; if it's 5, the second maun be 9. Either wey a 9 appears in ane o the pincers - ye dinnae ken which, and ye dinnae need tae.

Sae nae cell that can see baith pincers can be a 9. Thae cells are usually the twa corners that complete the rectangle."

"Inside ane box, find a digit that can only gang in twa or three cells, and check whether they aw sit in the same row, or aw in the same column. If they dae, the digit is definitely somewhaur alang that line - ye dinnae ken whaur, but ye ken it\'s inside this box. Sae it cannae be onywhere else alang the same line ootwith the box.\n\nThis places naething by itsel. It clears candidates oot o the wey sae that a single appears somewhaur else."

"Look alang ane row, column or box for cells wi juist a few candidates left. Tak %1$s o them and pool their candidates. If the pool has exactly %2$s digits in it, thae %3$s digits are spoken for: they hae tae gang in thae %4$s cells in some order, even though ye cannae yet say which goes whaur.

That's eneuch. Every ither cell in the unit can gie thae digits up, and it's usually ane o thae cells that then becomes a single.

The cells dinnae aw need the same candidates - {2,7}, {2,9} and {7,9} is a perfectly guid triple, and is the ane fowk miss."

"Look for cells haudin the same twa candidates - say {4,9} - that form a chain, ilk ane seein the next. Three isnae eneuch; ye need at least fower.

Colour them alternately as ye gang. Because ilk cell sees the next, nae twa neighbours can haud the same digit, sae the chain reads 4, 9, 4, 9 the hale wey alang - or 9, 4, 9, 4, and ye cannae tell which.

Either wey, twa cells o opposite colours haud different digits atween them: ane is the 4 and ane is the 9. Sae onything that can see baith o them can be neither, and loses baith candidates at ance.

The pattern is easy tae spot precisely because every cell in it looks the same. Follae the identical pairs roond the grid and see whaur they touch."

"Look for three cells haudin the same twa candidates - say {1,6} - that sit at three corners o a rectangle. The rectangle has tae lie in exactly twa boxes: twa rows and twa columns crossin twa boxes, no fower.

Noo look at the fowert corner. If it held only 1 and 6 as weel, the puzzle wad hae twa answers - ye could swap the 1s and 6s roond the rectangle and awthing else wad still work. A properly set puzzle has ane answer, sae the fowert corner maun be usin something else: its ither candidates stay, and 1 and 6 gang.

This is the ane argument in the book that's aboot the setter raither than the grid. It's sound on a published puzzle and worthless on ane ye've awready filled in wrangly, because then there may be nae answer at aw tae be unique."

"Pick a digit and look doon the rows for the anes whaur it has exactly twa cells left. Tak twa sic rows and see whether ane o their cells lands in the same column.

If it does, thae twa cells are in the same column and cannae baith haud the digit. Sae at least ane o the far ends does - the twa cells at the ither side. Ye dinnae ken which, and ye dinnae need tae: ony cell that can see baith far ends can gie the digit up.

Then dae it again wi columns instead o rows. The shape is a tall buildin wi a short ane beside it, which is whaur the name comes fae and hou ye spot it ance ye've seen a few."

"Pick a digit. Find a row whaur it has exactly twa places and a column whaur it has exactly twa places. Noo check whether ane cell o the row and ane cell o the column sit in the same box.

If they dae, thae twa cannae baith be the digit - ane box, ane digit. Sae at least ane o the twa remainin ends is, and onything seein baith ends can gie the digit up.

The reason fowk miss this ane is that there's naething tae line up: the fower cells mak a lopsided shape, and the only thing haudin it thegither is the box the twa inner ends share."

"Pick an empty cell and run through 1 tae 9, crossin aff onything that awready appears in its row, its column or its box. If exactly ane digit survives, it goes there.\n\nThis is the technique every ither ane exists tae set up. Awthing harder is a wey o gettin some cell doon tae a single candidate, sae when a harder technique pays aff, look here next."

"Pick ane digit and ignore every ither. Gang doon the rows and note the anes whaur that digit has juist twa or three possible cells left. Look for %1$s sic rows whase cells line up in the same %2$s columns.

If ye find them, ilk ane o thae %3$s rows maun pit the digit in ane o thae columns, and nae twa can use the same column. Sae atween them they use up the digit in aw %4$s columns - and every ither cell in thae columns can gie it up.

Then dae the hale thing again wi columns and rows swapped. Hauf o thir are found the second wey roond, and it's the hauf maist fowk never look for."

"Tak ane digit and mark every unit whaur it has exactly twa cells left. Thae twa are a see-saw: ane o them is the digit and the ither isnae.

Start onywhere and colour a cell, say, blue. Colour its see-saw pairtner green, then whate'er that ane is paired wi blue again, and keep gaun till the chain runs oot. Every blue cell is true or every green cell is - ye cannae tell which, and that is eneuch for twa things.

First: gin twa cells o the same colour turn up in ane raw, column or box, that colour is impossible, sae the digit gangs frae every cell wearin it and the ither colour is the answer throughout.

Second: ony cell ootside the chain that can see a blue and a green can gie the digit up, because ane o thae twa is haudin it whichever wey the chain faws.

It is slow wi a pencil and worth it: ane colourin aften clears a digit aff hauf the board."

"Tak ane digit and ane unit at a time - say, whaur can a 4 gang in this box? Score oot every cell in the unit that awready has a digit, or that sees a 4 in its ain raw or column. Gin ane cell is left, the 4 gangs there.\n\nThe trap is that ye cannae see this by lookin at the cell: it may happily accept five ither digits tae, sae naethin aboot it looks forced. Look at the digit insteid o the cell, and it appears immediately."

"Wark digit by digit raither than cell by cell. For ane unit, write doon whaur each missin digit could still gang. Then look for %1$s digits whase lists atween them cover only %2$s cells.

Thae %3$s digits hae tae fill thae %4$s cells, sae everythin else in them can be scored oot - which aften produces a naked single in ane o them or a naked pair across twa o them on the spot.

This is the ane folk find hardest, because there is naethin tae see whan ye look at the cells: they still hae plenty o candidates. The pattern is in the digits."

"Wark only wi cells that hae exactly twa candidates left.

Start at ane, say {2,6}, and suppose it isnae the 2 - then it is the 6. Move tae a cell it can see that has a 6 an aw, say {6,4}: that ane cannae be the 6, sae it is the 4. Move tae a cell that ane sees haudin a 4, and carry on, each step forced by the ane afore.

Gin ye reach a cell whase ither digit is 2 - the digit ye startit by rulin oot - ye are done. Either the first cell wis a 2 efter aw, or the chain ran and the last cell is a 2. Ane end or the ither hauds it, sae onything seein baith ends cannae.

Keep the chains short. Fower or five cells is findable wi a pencil; past that ye are daein bookkeepin, and a forcing chain is the honest name for it."
